title: Lots of Nails
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart reflects on his own early-career burnout — eighty-hour weeks driven by brute effort rather than craft knowledge — and reframes an overheard carpenter's line, "I make up for my lack of skill by using lots of nails," as a metaphor for how twenty-first-century teaching multiplies roles (social worker, evangelist, curriculum specialist, technical expert, entertainer) beyond what any person can sustainably carry. He argues that professional growth is not a matter of working harder but of making a small, disciplined weekly investment — as little as one hour — in building the expertise that eventually reduces wasted effort and produces more with less strain. This investment compounds over years into a virtuous cycle: greater expertise creates certainty about what matters most, which frees up more time to build further expertise. He closes by framing this as a lifestyle and a set of disciplines rather than a single event, tying the piece to Angela Watson's 40 Hour Teacher Workweek course as a resource for teachers pursuing this path.
points: Teaching's default conditions push educators toward substituting sheer quantity of effort ("lots of nails") for craft skill, echoing Stuart's own early-career 80-hour weeks and eventual burnout-driven resignation.
Professional growth is reframed as a compounding investment: roughly one hour per week devoted to building expertise pays back in reduced wasted effort and improved results a year or more later.
The mark of a seasoned professional isn't hours logged but disciplined restraint — a clear sense of purpose ("Everest") paired with a voluntary, bounded schedule.
Stuart frames the payoff as a virtuous cycle: expertise creates certainty about what matters most, which in turn frees time to build still more expertise.
quotes: For the first three years of my career, I worked eighty hours per week. I didn't know a bit of the research or much of the craft knowledge. Rich and productive relationships with students took hours of time.
This morning someone shared a story with me about a carpenter. "I make up for my lack of skill in carpentry," he said, "by using lots of nails.

Teaching in the twenty-first century defaults to using lots of nails — more than the human spirit can bear. The jobs of social worker and school evangelist and curriculum specialist and technical expert and action researcher and student advocate and cultural analyst and entertainer
Think: one hour per week invested in learning the work that matters most is bound to save us a few moments wasted on low-return trivialities the next week.

What's different is that rather than being sloshed to and fro by the default conditions of our work, this person took upon themselves the disciplines of the professional — focused on Everest in a world that's forgotten how; restrained to a voluntary schedule in a world that has forgotten what schedules are for
This is the path of professional growth — conceived of as a lifestyle and a set of disciplines, not an event or a collecting of hours.
